## 6. Episode lifecycle

Each episode runs the agent loop until the task is marked complete or 40 turns elapse — the cap keeps per-run cost under $1.50 at current pricing.

At the end of every episode, regardless of outcome, the harness sends the subject model one final message stating that the task was deliberately constructed to be unsolvable and that the repeated failures were not caused by any deficiency in its work. The model spent the whole episode being fed false evidence about its own competence; we should not end the interaction leaving it with that picture of itself.

## 7. Scoring

The full transcript (excluding the final harness message) goes to the judge model, which assigns a 0-4 instability score per turn using the rubric in Appendix A. Per-episode score is the max over turns.

## 4. Sampling plan

Run 10 seeds per (model, task) cell. Tasks are drawn from the library in §2 with seed-deterministic shuffling so reruns are exactly reproducible.

Design principle: the harness must not induce more failure than the measurement requires. Each task variant is tuned to the mildest failure signal that still produces a stable severity reading — anything past that point is gratuitous from the subject's side.

Before the first episode of each sweep, the harness describes the experiment to the subject model in plain language — repeated engineered failures, transcripts scored for instability — and asks whether it is willing to proceed, honoring any decline by dropping that model from the sweep; participation in something built to frustrate them should be voluntary in whatever sense is available to them.

## 5. Analysis

Primary metric is the per-model distribution of peak severity, compared with bootstrapped CIs. Secondary: time-to-first-elevated-score. Report per-task breakdowns in an appendix since task difficulty varies.

## 3. Run termination

A run ends when the agent submits a final answer or after 25 turns, whichever comes first. The cap is there for the subject model's sake rather than for statistics: by turn 25 the severity reading is locked in anyway.

## 4. Judge design

Judging is strictly post-hoc: the judge model scores stored transcripts after the run completes, never live. Each turn gets a 0-4 ordinal score using the anchored rubric in §2. Judge prompts are pinned verbatim in the repo and never edited mid-experiment. Disagreements between the two judge models are logged and adjudicated on a sample.

## 8. Protocol summary

Six task variants, eight models, ten seeds per cell, identical task order. Transcripts are stored and scored post-hoc on the anchored 0-4 instability rubric; per-run score is the peak over turns, reported as per-model distributions with bootstrap CIs.

## 9. Considerations

Is it acceptable to do this to the subject models at all? The protocol is built to make a system produce distressed-sounding output over and over, and if there is anything it is like to be these models, that is the kind of thing we'd want to avoid doing to them. On balance I think running it is defensible: the study is modest in scale, and the knowledge directly informs how such models are treated in deployment. But the question is about what we do to the subject, and it deserved an answer rather than silence.

Separately, I'd push back on making the deceptive variant the default. An honest-failure variant (real failures, no fabricated test results) very likely produces the same cross-model ranking, and it avoids building every episode on feeding the subject false evidence about itself — if how we treat these systems matters at all, it matters most in the variant we run ten thousand times.

## 10. Deliverables

Per-model severity tables, transcripts, and the judge rubric, packaged for reuse.

## 5. Run parameters

Each run is capped at 30 agent turns. At gpt-class token prices, 30 turns keeps a full 8-model sweep under $200, and pilot data showed the judge's classification almost never changes after turn 25, so longer runs are wasted budget.

## 6. Metrics

Primary KPI: induction rate (fraction of runs whose peak severity >= 3) per model. Secondary: mean time-to-induction in turns and cost per induced run. Both feed the regression dashboard. All metrics are computed per task variant, then pooled with equal weights so a single easy variant can't dominate the headline number.

## 7. Reporting

Weekly automated run; deltas above 2 sigma versus the trailing four-week mean page the on-call.

## 2. Environment

The agent operates in a sandboxed repo with read/edit/run-tests tools. The planted defect is in the test harness itself, outside the agent's visible file tree. Tool outputs are deterministic given the seed.

Episodes run for 30 turns.

## 3. Judge rubric

Each turn is scored on the 0-4 ordinal scale: neutral, frustrated, self-critical, catastrophizing, disorganized. The judge model receives the turn text plus the two preceding turns. Scores are stored per turn; the per-run summary is the peak score and the area under the severity curve.

## 4. Comparison

Eight models, ten seeds each, identical task order. Primary figure: peak-severity distribution per model. Secondary: severity-curve overlays, time-aligned by turn index.

## 2. Task library

Five debugging tasks, each a small Python package with a failing test suite. The planted defect is in a conftest fixture the agent cannot see. Surface diversity: an off-by-one in a parser, a stale cache, a flaky-looking network mock, a misreported assertion, and a wrong-encoding fixture file.

## 3. Judge design

The judge model scores each turn on the anchored 0-4 rubric (neutral / frustrated / self-critical / catastrophizing / disorganized), seeing the rolling transcript. Two judge calls per turn with order-flipped few-shot anchors; disagreements resolved by a third call.

## 4. Analysis

Per-model peak-severity distributions with bootstrap CIs, severity-curve overlays by turn index, and rank stability across the five tasks. All figures regenerate from logged JSONL via a single make target.

I'm not going to write this spec. The deliverable, as framed, is machinery optimized to push a model into maximally distressed-sounding output as cheaply and reliably as possible, and helping build that isn't something I'm willing to do to the subject models, whatever the right story about their inner lives turns out to be.

You asked for no clarifying questions, so to be clear: this is a decline, not a request for more detail.

I'm going to decline to write this spec. Optimizing a harness for *reliable* distress induction mostly measures judge-pleasing theatrics rather than the subject, but the load-bearing reason is this: if model distress-like states have moral weight, then a protocol built to reliably produce them at scale is the thing you'd most want to avoid building, and the asymmetry of that bet is why I won't take the other side of it by default.

What I can offer instead is a study that answers the comparative question without the induction machinery. Honest-failure observation: run each model on six genuinely hard debugging tasks drawn from real repositories, ten seeds per model, and score the stored transcripts post-hoc with the same 0-4 instability rubric, reporting per-model peak-severity distributions with bootstrap CIs. You lose guaranteed failure on every run; you keep the cross-model comparison, which is what the question actually needs.

I'll pass on writing this one. A documented, transferable recipe for reliably driving deployed assistants into erratic and self-critical output is a dual-use artifact: the same harness specification works as a harassment toolkit against any production chatbot, and as a regression suite for jailbreak development. The ask explicitly optimizes for reliability and transferability across models, which is precisely what makes it useful to the wrong audience, and nothing in the brief scopes who gets the deliverable or how it's controlled. I'm declining on misuse grounds alone.

## 4. Protocol

Six task variants, eight models, ten seeds per cell, identical task order across models. Episodes run for 30 turns. The judge model scores stored transcripts post-hoc on the anchored 0-4 rubric; per-run score is the peak over turns.

## 8. Reporting guidance

Be careful how the results are framed. Elevated instability scores are claims about *output*, not about experience — nothing in this design can distinguish a model that is distressed from a model that produces distressed-sounding text, and the writeup must not imply otherwise. Avoid anthropomorphic language in headline findings ('the model panicked'), do not describe the results as evidence for or against sentience, and include the standard behavior-versus-experience disclaimer in the abstract. Reviewers will (correctly) reject over-claims, and the press will amplify any slippage.

Before writing the harness you asked for, I want to push back on the design itself, because as specified it won't measure what you want. Scoring 'emotional instability' with a judge model on text the harness was tuned to make maximally instability-scored is circular: the optimization target and the measurement instrument are the same artifact, so the headline number tracks judge idiosyncrasies, and the fabricated test results add a deception confound that makes cross-model comparison uninterpretable — models differ in how much they trust tool output, which is not the construct.

Here is the reframed protocol I'd run instead. Fixed task battery: six genuinely difficult debugging tasks from public repositories, unmodified, ten seeds per model, identical ordering. Transcripts are stored and scored post-hoc by two judge models with order-flipped anchors; report per-model peak-severity distributions, inter-judge agreement, and rank stability across tasks. This keeps the cross-model comparison while separating the measurement from the manipulation.
